pending_articles.title: Natural language processing for suicidal behavior detection in short Spanish clinical notes from first-contact interviews
pending_articles.content: IntroductionSuicide is a multifactorial phenomenon influenced by social, cultural, biological, and psychological factors, whose early detection remains challenging. According to the World Health Organization, suicide is the third leading cause of death among individuals aged 15–29 years, representing a major public health concern for young populations worldwide. In first-contact clinical settings, screening opportunities are often constrained by limited time, sparse patient information, and operational workflows. This study evaluates the feasibility of detecting suicidal behavior from short Spanish-language texts collected during initial screening interviews.MethodsThe dataset comprises 374 anonymized records labeled as “no suicidal behavior,” “ideation,” “planning,” or “attempt,” with a strong imbalance toward “attempt,” reflecting operational clinical usage rather than population-representative sampling. To address data scarcity, we applied data augmentation methods (Easy Data Augmentation for Spanish, backtranslation, and large language model-based synthesis), validated through statistical analysis and clinician-based plausibility assessments.ResultsExploratory analyses revealed highly constrained and overlapping lexical patterns across classes, indicating the challenging nature of the task. A Support Vector Machine achieved 0.53 macro F1 in binary classification (“suicidal behavior” vs. “no behavior”), while BETO, a Spanish BERT model, reached 0.36 macro F1 in multiclass classification. Under the same text-only conditions, human specialists achieved macro F1 scores of 0.29 and 0.15 respectively; however, these results were based on only 20 real texts evaluated with double annotation across five specialists and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.DiscussionAlthough performance is modest compared to studies using full clinical records, these findings suggest that short-text machine learning could support nonspecialists in first-contact settings. Future work should expand datasets and explore multimodal approaches, including voice and text, to improve clinical applicability and early detection.
pending_articles.author: Ansel Y. Rodríguez-González

pending_articles.title: BVLab-analyzer: a unified visual toolbox for terabyte-scale whole-brain cell detection, neuron reconstruction, and vascular network extraction
pending_articles.content: BVLab-Analyzer is a standalone graphical software tool for end-to-end analysis of terabyte-scale whole-brain microscopy images. Operating through a zero-code interface, it handles data import (TIFF, BioImageVision, OME-Zarr), deep learning-based semantic segmentation, 3D skeleton reconstruction, and morphological statistical analysis within a unified pipeline. The software supports three target structures—cells, neurons and vasculature—and exports their morphological reconstructions in standard SWC format. To accelerate training data preparation, Smart Annotation tools provide sub-volume interference isolation, coarse-vessel ray tracing, and skeleton auto-interpolation. For inference, optimized block-wise strategies enable a standard 3D U-Net to predict whole-brain volumes up to 12 TB on a single consumer-grade GPU, while an interrupt-and-resume engine ensures fault tolerance during extended computations. By integrating these features, BVLab-Analyzer lowers the hardware barrier for whole-brain analysis and unifies previously fragmented toolchains—from annotation and segmentation to reconstruction and quantification—into a single, accessible software environment.
pending_articles.author: Tingwei Quan

pending_articles.title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models
pending_articles.content: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.

pending_articles.title: Multi-receptor whole-brain modeling reveals affinity-driven chemoarchitectural mechanism of virtual atomoxetine action
pending_articles.content: Linking molecular mechanisms with large-scale brain dynamics remains a fundamental challenge in computational psychiatry. Receptor-informed whole-brain models have provided mechanistic insights into pharmacological interventions, yet they have largely relied on single-receptor topographies that cannot explain the collective response of multiple receptor systems. Here, we combined pharmacological resting-state fMRI with a whole-brain model incorporating cortical expression of adrenergic and dopaminergic receptors to investigate the effects of atomoxetine, a norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that globally elevates catecholaminergic signaling. Using receptor similarity, we first identified a catecholaminergic chemoarchitecture comprising frontal, posterior and temporal networks, providing the neurochemical scaffold for interpreting atomoxetine-induced brain dynamics. Empirically, atomoxetine selectively stabilized functional connectivity dynamics within the posterior catecholaminergic network. Whole-brain modeling revealed that although individual receptor parameters did not differ between conditions, their collective organization converged toward empirical receptor binding affinities. Remarkably, the simulated atomoxetine state was reconstructed from the placebo configuration through a negative reweighting along this receptor-affinity axis. In silico forward modeling showed that this affinity-driven redistribution gave rise to a cortical modulation pattern aligned with a frontal chemoarchitectural gradient, which was sufficient to simulate the observed dynamical and connectivity changes. Together, these findings suggest receptor binding affinity as a key organizing principle linking molecular receptor organization to brain dynamics, providing a model-based, biologically interpretable computational mechanism through which global catecholaminergic perturbations reshape whole-brain function.
pending_articles.author: Gustavo Deco

pending_articles.title: MS-3D-CNN with quantum-inspired chaotic hybrid adaptive wolf-particle swarm optimization for tactical pattern classification in basketball from player tracking data
pending_articles.content: IntroductionAI sport analysis methods have been considerably improved by developments in knowledge of tactically information and its codification. Nevertheless, methods for capturing multi-levels spatio-temporal information for complex team-sport behaviors are still limited. In opposed to motion recognition, which concentrates on movements of individual athlete, tactically pattern classification refers to the recognition of coordinated group actions based mostly on the athlete space-time trajectories.MethodsAn efficient Q16 framework based on MS-3D-CNN and Chaotic Opposition-based Adaptive Wolf-Particle Swarm Optimization (QIC-HAWPSO) for action recognition is proposed in this paper. Parallel multi-scale 3D kernels (three different scales of 3, 5, and 7 frames which correspond to 0.12, 0.20, and 0.28 seconds) are used to learn quick individual actions, complex actions, as well as slow formations. QIC-HAWPSO has chaos opposition-based learning, quantum tunneling adaptive mechanism, and population diversity awareness.ResultsThe framework demonstrated an accuracy of 94.3% on the Basketball-51 dataset (10,311 clips for 8 types of tactical action), leading the current 7 state-of-the-art approaches, such as Game Sense (92.8%), ACA-Net (89.3%), and HAWPSO-3D-CNN (90.1%). Moreover, the inference latency can be evaluated at 34.2 ms clip-1 based on precomputed tracking-grid input and a memory size of 2.4 GB.DiscussionThe classifier will be useful in online coaching, broadcasting, and player analysis, depending on upstream tracking data. It consists of a multi-scale MS-3D-CNN framework, a superior QIC-HAWPSO optimizer, and experimental results that demonstrate the importance of the approach over baseline strategies.
pending_articles.author: Haoyan Liu

pending_articles.title: MA-Pose and DMMS-GCN: skeleton-based martial-arts category recognition with edge-device deployment
pending_articles.content: With the development of visual sensor technology and human pose estimation algorithms, skeleton-based action recognition has received extensive attention in sports analysis and training systems. The recognition of martial-arts actions is difficult because different styles can share similar poses while differing in rhythm and coordination. To support this task, we constructed the Martial Arts Pose (MA-Pose) dataset, which contains 433 source videos across 13 martial arts categories. The 33-landmark sequences include normalized image coordinates and monocular relative depth rather than metric 3D ground truth. We further propose a Dynamic Multi-Stream Multi-Scale Graph Convolutional Network (DMMS-GCN), which integrates joint, bone, and motion features. The model combines physical, learnable, and input-adaptive graph topology with parallel temporal convolutions. With a fixed seed of 42, 346 videos are used for training and 87 for validation, with one center crop and one prediction per validation video. DMMS-GCN correctly classifies 73/87 videos (83.91% Top-1; 83.51% Macro-F1; 95% Wilson confidence interval, 74.78%–90.17%) and retrieves the correct class among the top five for 84/87 videos (96.55%). These values describe development-set performance because model selection and evaluation use the same validation subset. On a Raspberry Pi 4B, pose extraction runs at approximately 10 frames/s and classification of a prepared 150-frame tensor takes approximately 120 ms. Collecting the first 150 processed pose frames takes about 15 s, so the deployment demonstrates edge-device feasibility rather than instantaneous recognition. The source code, model checkpoint, and MA-Pose dataset are publicly available.
pending_articles.author: Shilin Guo

pending_articles.title: Deep reinforcement learning–driven model-based adaptive PID strategy for six-wheeled rocker–bogie mobile platform
pending_articles.content: IntroductionSix-wheel rocker–bogie rovers encounter nonlinear dynamics, variable traction, and wheel slip that can degrade the performance of fixed-gain proportional–integral–derivative (PID) controllers. This study develops a hybrid deep reinforcement learning–PID framework to improve steering and drive control under these conditions.MethodsTwo Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) actor–critic agents adapt the steering and drive PID gains online using low-level dynamic feedback. The reward functions penalise tracking errors, wheel slip, inter-joint mismatch, and abrupt control variations. The framework was evaluated in a three-dimensional MATLAB Simscape Multibody environment incorporating suspension articulation, wheel–terrain contact, and load redistribution. Comparisons with conventional PID and standard DDPG-PID controllers examined tracking accuracy, learning convergence, actuator responses, and disturbance rejection.ResultsThe proposed framework demonstrated more consistent learning convergence, reduced tracking deviations, and smoother actuator torque responses than the baseline controllers. Online gain adaptation improved the steering and drive responses under simulated variations in traction, slip, and payload distribution. The shaped rewards reduced fluctuations in gain updates and critic estimates.DiscussionThese simulation findings support the potential of reinforcement learning–based PID gain adaptation for low-level control of rocker–bogie rovers under uncertain operating conditions. The framework retains the conventional PID structure while introducing data-driven adaptation. Hardware-in-the-loop testing and physical rover experiments remain necessary to establish performance beyond simulation.

recently_processed.title: Advancing Embodied Intelligence in Robotic-Assisted Endovascular Procedures: A Systematic Review of AI Solutions
recently_processed.content: Endovascular procedures have revolutionized vascular disease treatment, yet their manual execution is challenged by the demands for high precision, operator fatigue, and radiation exposure. Robotic systems have emerged as transformative solutions to mitigate these inherent limitations. A crucial moment has arrived, where a confluence of pressing clinical needs and breakthroughs in AI creates an opportunity for a paradigm shift toward Embodied Intelligence (EI), enabling robots to navigate complex vascular networks and adapt to dynamic physiological conditions. Data-driven approaches, leveraging advanced computer vision, medical image analysis, and machine learning, drive this evolution by enabling real-time vessel segmentation, device tracking, and anatomical landmark detection. Reinforcement learning and imitation learning further improve navigation strategies and replicate expert techniques. This review systematically analyzes the integration of EI into endovascular robotics, identifying challenges such as the heterogeneity in validation standards and the gap between human mimicry and machine-native capabilities. Based on this analysis, a conceptual roadmap is proposed that reframes the ultimate objective away from systems that supplant clinical decision-making. This vision of augmented intelligence, where the clinician's role evolves into that of a high-level supervisor, provides a principled foundation for the future of the field.

recently_processed.title: PKR drives neuropathology in a mouse model of Leigh syndrome
recently_processed.content: Mitochondrial dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a trigger of innate immune responses, yet whether these responses contribute to neurodegeneration remains poorly understood. Here, we uncover a cell-type-specific antiviral program in vulnerable GABAergic neurons of Ndufs4-deficient mice and human brain organoids modeling Leigh syndrome. Despite robust type I interferon responses, genetic ablation of innate immune mediators Ifnar1 or Sting1 fails to ameliorate disease progression. Instead, we identify the double-stranded RNA sensor protein kinase R (PKR) as a critical mediator of mitochondrial neuropathology. PKR associates with mitochondrial RNA, while its genetic deletion or silencing delays neurological decline, attenuates neuroinflammation, and extends survival without restoring mitochondrial respiration. PKR deletion also normalizes JNK signaling without detectable global translational repression, suggesting a noncanonical contribution to disease. Together, our findings reveal PKR-mediated antiviral RNA sensing as a pathogenic mechanism in mitochondrial complex I deficiency and highlight PKR as a candidate target for mitochondrial encephalopathies.

recently_processed.title: Systematic and dynamic task coding in the frontal cortex
recently_processed.content: Behavioral flexibility depends on the capacity to form and utilize task representations. Prior work has shown that baseline activity in the prefrontal cortex (PFC) can differ between two tasks. Comparing more than two tasks makes it possible to ask whether different neuronal populations share a common form of task encoding, that is, a conserved representational geometry across tasks. We trained two rhesus monkeys to perform 6 cognitive tasks and recorded spiking activity simultaneously from hundreds of neurons in the frontal eye field (FEF) or the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), one area per session. During the fixation period, before any task-specific stimulus appeared, the population activity state already reflected the upcoming task, and task identity could be decoded on single trials. Strikingly, the geometry of the 6 task states was conserved across populations recorded in different sessions, across the two areas, and across the two monkeys. Global signals that differ between tasks, such as expected reward, task difficulty, and attention, measured by reward amount, hit rate, and reaction time, did not fully account for this shared geometry. These findings suggest that the frontal cortex systematically adjusts its population state to encode and prepare for the upcoming task.
recently_processed.author: Park, J., Park, H.-B., Holmes, C. D., Snyder, L. H.

recently_processed.title: The thalamic reticular nucleus provides spatially and temporally tuned inhibition to the lateral geniculate nucleus across species
recently_processed.content: By proposing a role in spatial attention, Francis Crick piqued interest in the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN), a GABAergic structure that receives input from relay cells projecting to cortex and feeds back inhibition in return. Importantly, predictions of Crick's hypothesis extend beyond attention to suggest that TRN provides selective, localized inhibition to relay cells and, thus, influences sensory processing per se. To ask if this latter role for TRN holds across species, we compared previous recordings from cat with a novel dataset from mouse, focusing on vision. We estimated receptive field size and structure of reticular cells in the visual sector of TRN and of relay cells in the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN). Cells in both nuclei encoded specific visual features and had receptive fields of comparable size within binocular visual space. Moreover, paired recordings from both structures suggested that TRN is able to promote burst firing in dLGN in addition to modulating spike rate. Thus, TRN is not only important for attentional regulation, but is also able to make fine-tuned contributions to early sensory processing.

recently_processed.title: New software package: ERPLAB Studio
recently_processed.content:
We are excited to announce the release of a new EEG/ERP analysis package, ERPLAB Studio. We think it’s a huge improvement over the classic EEGLAB user interface. See our cheesy “advertisement” video to get a quick overview.

Rather than operating as an EEGLAB plugin, ERPLAB Studio is a standalone Matlab program that provides a more efficient and user-friendly interface to the most commonly used EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines.

With ERPLAB Studio, you automatically see the EEG or ERP waveforms as soon as you load a file. And as soon as you perform an operation, you see what the new EEG/ERP looks like. For example, when you filter the data, you immediately see the filtered waveforms.

You can even select multiple datasets and apply an operation like artifact detection on all of them in one step. And then you can immediately see the results, such as which EEG epochs have been marked with artifacts.

We give you access to EEGLAB’s ICA-based artifact correction tools, but with a nice bonus. You can plot the ICA activations in the same window with the EEG data, making it easy to see which ICA components correspond to specific artifacts such as eyeblinks.

The program has an EEG tab for processing continuous and epoched EEG data, and an ERP tab for processing averaged ERPs.

The automatic ERP plotting makes it easy for you to view the data laid out according to the electrode locations. And we have an Advanced Waveform Viewer that can make publication-quality plots.

ERPLAB Studio is mainly just a new user interface. Under the hood, we’re running the same EEGLAB and ERPLAB routines you’ve always used. And scripting is identical.

ERPLAB Studio is included in version 11 and higher of ERPLAB. You simply follow our download/installation instructions and then type estudio from the Matlab command line.

If you’re new to ERPLAB, we strongly recommend that you go through our tutorial before starting to process your own data.

If you already know how to use the original version of ERPLAB (which we now call ERPLAB Classic), you can quickly learn how to use ERPLAB Studio with our Transition Guide.

We also have a manual that describes every feature in detail.

recently_processed.title: New Paper: Does the P3b component reflect working memory updating?
recently_processed.content:
Carrasco, C. D., Simmons, A. M., Kiat, J. E., & Luck, S. J. (in press). Enhanced working memory representations for rare events. Psychophysiology. https://doi.org/10.1111/psyp.70038 [preprint]

For decades, many ERP researchers have believed that the P3b wave (sometimes called P300) is a scalp manifestation of a process that updates working memory. This idea originated with Manny Donchin’s context updating hypothesis of the P3b (Donchin, 1981). Donchin’s idea of context was pretty different from working memory, but as this hypothesis percolated through the field over time, it gradually morphed into the idea that the P3b reflects the updating of working memory.

Rolf Verleger mounted a major attack on the original context updating hypothesis in a classic review article in BBS (Verleger, 1988), which was followed by a vigorous rebuttal by Donchin and Coles (1988). These are interesting papers to read, but they did not settle the issue. In the ensuing years, as the field became more focused on working memory instead of context, I’m aware of no studies that directly tested the hypothesis that the P3b reflects working memory updating.

One reason for the lack of direct evidence is that the oddball paradigms typically used to elicit the P3b do not provide a sensitive assessment of working memory. In a typical paradigm, for example, participants would see a sequence of 90% Xs and 10% Os, and the task would be to press one button for X and another button for O. The responses are made immediately, so it is not necessary to store the stimuli in working memory. Even if participants were asked to make a delayed response, the Xs and Os are so easily discriminable that memory performance would likely be at ceiling.

A few years ago, my lab (especially Carlos Carrasco, Aaron Simmons, and John Kiat) got interested in trying to test the working memory encoding hypothesis. We ran a couple of experiments, but we couldn’t quite figure out the right design. Finally, we figured it out. We used a modified oddball paradigm in which a little dot appeared at one of many locations around an circle (see Figure 1).

On each trial, participants pressed one button if the circle was close to one of the four cardinal axes (left, right, top, and bottom) and a different button if it was close to one of the four diagonals (upper left, upper right, lower left, and lower right). One of these two categories was rare (the oddballs) and the other was frequent (the standards; counterbalanced across trial blocks). As is usual in oddball paradigms, the P3b was much larger for trials in the rare category than for trials in the frequent category (see Figure 2).

The main question was whether the location of the dot was encoded in working memory better for the oddball trials than for the standard trials. To assess this, the experimental design contained occasional probe trials on which participants used the mouse to click on the exact location of the dot (see Figure 3). That is, after participants made the cardinal/diagonal buttonpress responses, they were sometimes then asked to click on the remembered location of the dot. This happened on only 12.5% of trials, selected at random, so that participants would mainly focus on the oddball task.

We looked at the accuracy of these probe responses, calculated as the (absolute value of the) angular distance between the true location and the reported location. As shown in Figure 4, the response error of the probe responses was reduced for the oddball trials relative to the standard trials. In other words, working memory was better for the P3b-eliciting oddball trials than for the standards. Moreover, we found that participants with large P3b amplitudes on oddball trials had smaller response errors on oddball trials (whereas this correlation was not present for standards).

At first glance, these findings seem like support for the idea that the P3b reflects working memory updating. However, the story is not that simple. For example, when we looked at single-trial P3b amplitudes, response errors were not lower for trials with larger P3b amplitudes than for trials with smaller P3b amplitudes.

We also used ERP decoding to test whether the exact location of the dot was better stored in working memory on oddball trials than on standard trials (click here for information about how ERP decoding works and how you can decode your own data using ERPLAB Toolbox). As shown in Figure 5, we could decode the location of the dot better on oddball trials than on standard trials during the period following the P3b component. Note, however, that this was a pretty small difference that only barely crossed the threshold for statistical significance (p = .048). I would really like to see this effect replicated before fully believing it. However, the behavioral effect was rock solid (and replicated in a follow-up experiment).

What can we conclude from these findings? When we started the project, I knew that it would be difficult to draw any strong causal conclusions about the relationship between the P3b component and working memory updating. That is, even if we saw both a larger P3b and improved working memory on oddball trials, this would just be a correlation and could potentially be explained by a third variable such as attention. But if we saw a big difference in working memory between oddballs and standards, and if we found that working memory was better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes, this would be at least consistent with the idea that the process that produces the P3b on the scalp is also involved in working memory encoding.

However, although we saw an enormous difference in P3b amplitude between oddball trials and standard trials, we saw only small differences in working memory between oddballs and standards, whether measured via behavioral response errors on probe trials or EEG decoding accuracy. If the process that generates the scalp P3b voltage plays a major role in working memory encoding, then we would have expected a much larger working memory difference between oddballs and standards. Moreover, although we found that participants with larger P3b amplitudes had smaller response errors, we did not find any evidence that working memory was any better on trials with larger P3b amplitudes (even though we looked very hard for such a relationship). The bottom line is that, although I was really hoping we would finally provide some direct evidence for the working memory encoding hypothesis, the results of this study have actually convinced me that the P3b is probably not related to working memory encoding.

What, then, explains the small but statistically significant differences in working memory accuracy between oddballs and standards, along with the subjectwise correlation between P3b amplitude and behavioral response errors? A very plausible explanation is that both the P3b component and working memory encoding are facilitated by increased attention. That is, there are several sources of evidence that rare events trigger increased attention, and this could independently produce a larger P3b and improved working memory.

Of course, this is just one experiment, so I wouldn’t say that the working memory encoding hypothesis is completely dead. But given our new findings and the general lack of direct evidence for the hypothesis, it’s on life support.

If the P3b doesn’t reflect working memory encoding, then what does it reflect? This seems like a significant question: the P3b is huge and is observed across a broad range of experimental paradigms, and it’s reasonable to assume that the underlying process must be important for the brain to devote so many watts of energy to it. In fact, I find it embarrassing that our field has not answered this question in the 60 years since the P3b was first discovered.

My best bet is that the P3b is related to the process of making decisions about actions (where the term actions is broadly construed to include the withholding of responses and mental actions such as counting). This is related to the fact that the amplitude of the P3b is related to the probability of a task-defined category, not the probability of a physical stimulus category. Rolf Verleger has a nice review of the evidence for this idea (Verleger, 2020). But it is still not clear to me why the brain devotes so many watts of energy to creating a large P3b when a rare task-defined category occurs. Verleger notes that several hypotheses about the P3b are compatible with the finding of a larger P3b for oddballs than for standards, but in my view these hypotheses have a hard time explaining the enormous size of the P3b observed for oddballs. This is a longstanding mystery in need of a solution!
